title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
notes: Annotated by hand from the paper. The degradation problem (Fig. 4) is the claim most worth testing at reduced scale: it is a comparison between two architectures of equal depth, and the effect is about optimisation rather than about scale.

claims.text: Plain networks show higher training error as depth increases, and residual networks of the same depth do not.
claims.notes: The degradation problem. Both arms are small convnets on an image dataset, so this shrinks cleanly.

claims.text: A 34-layer residual network reaches lower validation error than an 18-layer one, while the plain 34-layer network is worse than the plain 18-layer one.
claims.notes: Same effect as above, stated as a depth comparison.

claims.text: The 152-layer residual network reaches 3.57% top-5 error on the ImageNet test set.
claims.notes: A headline number; not reproducible at reduced scale by construction.

claims.text: Identity shortcuts perform comparably to projection shortcuts while adding no parameters.
claims.notes: The paper reports a small difference between options A, B and C. At reduced scale with few seeds this is likely below the noise floor, so inconclusive is the honest expectation.

claims.text: Residual networks converge faster in the early stages of training than plain networks of the same depth.
claims.notes: Convergence speed, measurable within a few epochs.

claims.text: A 1202-layer residual network performs worse than the 110-layer one on CIFAR-10, which the paper attributes to overfitting.
claims.notes: Depends on training a 1202-layer network, which is far outside a small CPU budget.
